abstracts.abstract: Human-machine collaboration increasingly relies on adaptive automation systems, yet existing frameworks treat human cognitive states as passive inputs rather than active co-regulatory variables. This paper proposes a new paradigm—Cognitive Co-Regulation Theory (CCRT)—which reconceptualizes human-automation interaction as a bidirectional regulatory process where both the human operator and the automation system continuously negotiate and share control authority based on real-time cognitive state inference. CCRT integrates Dynamic Systems Theory with Computational Rationality to model how mental workload, situation awareness, and trust jointly shape adaptive control boundaries. We formalize CCRT through a set of differential equations describing the coupled dynamics of human cognitive engagement and automation agency, demonstrating through analytical derivations that co-regulatory stability emerges only when both parties maintain sufficient transparency of intent. A simulation study varying cognitive state trajectories and automation transparency levels reveals three distinct co-regulatory regimes: seamless collaboration, oscillatory conflict, and graceful degradation. The paradigm shift from unilateral adaptation to mutual co-regulation fundamentally changes how human factors should be evaluated in supervisory control contexts. CCRT provides designers with a new theoretical lens for constructing automation systems that treat human cognitive engagement as a shared resource rather than a constraint to be managed, offering a foundational framework for the next generation of human-centered automation research.

Keystroke-Level Models (KLM) have long served as foundational tools for predicting human performance time in human-computer and human-robot interaction tasks. However, existing KLM variants for robotics fail to adequately account for the bidirectional communicative nature of social HRI, where robot feedback signals simultaneously serve as both task-relevant information and cognitive triggers that modulate operator behavior. This paper significantly extends the Cognitive Human-Robot Interaction Model (CHRIM), a GOMS-based analytical framework, by introducing Social Feedback Operators (SFOs) that represent robot-generated cues such as gesture, gaze direction, and verbal acknowledgment as first-class cognitive operators with empirically derived execution times. We contribute a comprehensive set of model parameters calibrated through three controlled experiments involving 78 participants performing collaborative manipulation tasks with a social service robot. The extended CHRIM with SFOs demonstrates substantially improved predictive accuracy (mean absolute error reduced by 34% compared to baseline GOMS-HRI) across task complexity levels and varying robot social cue configurations. Critically, the model now captures the attentional capture effect of robot gaze shifts and the trust calibration effects of progressive robot communication styles, phenomena that existing models cannot analytically represent. This work advances cognitive engineering tools for HRI by providing practitioners with a theoretically grounded, quantitatively validated model that bridges the gap between low-level motor operations and high-level social cognition in robot-assisted tasks.

Supervisory control of multiple heterogeneous robots in unstructured environments imposes extraordinary cognitive demands on human operators, and existing multi-robot interfaces remain anchored in paradigms designed for single-agent monitoring. This paper presents MetaMorph, a paradigm-innovative multi-robot supervisory interface that fundamentally rethinks the human-robot interaction model by shifting from agent-centric to mission-centric control abstraction. MetaMorph introduces Adaptive Mission Decomposition (AMD), a novel interaction paradigm where the system automatically decomposes high-level mission objectives into dynamically adjustable control hierarchies that map to operator cognitive capacities. The interface employs a tangible augmented reality overlay on physical workspace, allowing operators to manipulate mission parameters through spatial gestures while the underlying multi-robot coordination adapts in real time. We implemented MetaMorph on a testbed comprising aerial, wheeled, and manipulator robots performing coordinated infrastructure inspection. A 48-participant user study compared MetaMorph against a state-of-the-art multi-robot control interface across three mission complexity tiers. Results demonstrate that MetaMorph significantly reduces operator mental workload (NASA-TLX scores reduced by 41% at high complexity) while maintaining or improving task performance metrics including mission completion time and coverage accuracy. Notably, the paradigm shift to mission-centric abstraction enables graceful scaling: operators effectively supervised up to nine heterogeneous robots without performance degradation, compared to a ceiling of four agents in the baseline condition. MetaMorph establishes a new design paradigm for human-centered automation in complex multi-robot scenarios.

Wearable assistive exoskeletons for upper-limb rehabilitation face a persistent trade-off between mechanical rigidity, needed for effective load bearing, and compliance, needed for safe and comfortable human-machine coupling. Conventional impedance control approaches treat this as a tuning problem, but physical human-exoskeleton interaction remains sub-optimal because existing controllers cannot distinguish between intentional human movement corrections and involuntary muscle spasms or fatigue-induced tremors. This paper presents Adaptive Assistive Modulation (AAM), a significantly improved control architecture for upper-limb wearable systems that integrates real-time electromyography (EMG) signal classification with adaptive impedance control to dynamically distinguish voluntary human corrections from involuntary movements. AAM employs a hierarchical signal processing pipeline: low-level EMG pattern recognition identifies movement intent and classifies correction type, while a mid-level adaptive impedance regulator adjusts mechanical coupling stiffness within 15ms. The high-level supervisory module monitors long-term fatigue progression to proactively shift assistance levels. We implemented AAM on a custom-designed upper-limb exoskeleton and evaluated it with 24 post-stroke patients across 12 sessions. Significant improvements over baseline adaptive impedance control include 28% reduction in kinematic tracking error, 39% improvement in voluntary movement initiation time, and notably, a 52% reduction in adverse interaction events caused by involuntary movements. Participants also reported substantially higher comfort and trust ratings on standardized questionnaires. This work advances assistive technology by providing a practical, implementable control architecture that substantially improves safety and effectiveness of wearable rehabilitation systems.
